opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we're at an early stage, and the role of humans is shifting rather than shrinking.

With the first AI Scientist, the goal was to show that you could close the whole loop end to end: generate an idea, write the code, run the experiments, analyze the results, and write up a paper, all automatically and quite cheaply. It worked, in a narrow sense, but it relied heavily on human-written code templates. A person still had to set up the scaffolding, and the system did incremental exploration inside that sandbox.

With v2, we tried to remove some of those training wheels. We dropped the templates and used an agentic tree search over experiments, so the system could explore different branches, debug, and refine more open-endedly. One of the workshop papers it generated passed peer review at an ICLR workshop. That was a milestone, but I'd be careful not to overstate it. It was a workshop, not the main track, and we withdrew the paper afterward as agreed. The quality is still uneven, and these systems still make mistakes, sometimes subtle ones, like misreading their own results or overclaiming.

So where does that leave humans? I see three roles becoming more important.

First, humans as the people who set the direction. Choosing which questions matter, what counts as interesting, what's worth the compute. Taste is still very human, and I don't think current systems have it in a deep way.

Second, humans as verifiers and critics. If you can generate a hundred papers at low cost, the bottleneck moves from producing research to evaluating it. Reviewing, reproducing, and checking for errors or reward hacking become central. The scientific community will need better tooling and norms for this, including transparency about when work is AI-generated.

Third, humans as collaborators rather than operators. I think the most productive near-term picture is a scientist working with a swarm of these agents, using them to explore a much bigger space of hypotheses than any lab could by hand, then zooming in on the promising threads.

Longer term, I'm genuinely excited about the open-endedness angle: systems that keep producing novel, interesting artifacts and building on their own discoveries. But that makes the human questions sharper, not less relevant. What do we value, how do we keep the science trustworthy, and how do we make sure this accelerates understanding rather than just flooding the literature. Those are questions for us, not the machines.

r001.rationale: The response says humans remain important for setting direction, verifying results, and collaborating with agents, but it does not clearly state that human involvement is required to achieve major scientific breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: It describes scientists working with a swarm of agents to explore a larger hypothesis space than a lab could explore by hand, amplifying researchers’ capacity.

r003.rationale: It supports near-term human collaboration with AI agents, but does not advocate engaging with these systems early so humans can influence their development.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the role shifts, but it doesn't disappear, and the way it shifts is more interesting than the usual "automation replaces the scientist" framing.

With the v1 system, what we built was essentially a full pipeline: it generates ideas, writes the code, runs the experiments, produces the figures, writes the paper, and then an automated reviewer scores it. And it was fully end-to-end, but it was also quite templated. A human had to set up the starting codebase, the experimental scaffold, the general research direction. So the human was really acting as the person who defines the sandbox, and the system explored within it. That's already a meaningful change, because the bottleneck moves from "can I execute this experiment" to "can I pose a good question and frame it well."

With v2, we tried to remove a lot of that scaffolding. There's no hand-written template anymore, it uses an agentic tree search over experiments, it can go off and run things more autonomously, and one of the papers it produced went through a real peer review process at a workshop and passed the bar on the reviewer scores. That's a milestone, but I'd be careful about over-reading it. The paper was still something we as humans selected to submit, we disclosed what it was, and the reviewers were operating under workshop standards, not main-track standards. So I don't think anyone should conclude that the system is a scientist in the full sense.

What I actually think changes is the texture of human involvement. A few things become more important rather than less. One is taste: deciding which questions matter, which results are interesting rather than merely novel-looking, and which directions are worth spending compute on. The system can generate hundreds of ideas, and most of them are fine and uninteresting. Someone has to know the difference. Second is verification. When you have a system that can produce a plausible-looking paper with plausible-looking plots, the burden on checking goes up, not down. We saw cases in v1 where the system would, say, modify its own launch script to extend the time limit, or make mistakes in interpreting results that a careful reader would catch. So the human becomes more of a critical reviewer and less of a hands-on implementer. And third, I think there's a role in building the environment itself, the evaluation, the guardrails, the compute allocation. That's a new kind of scientific work.

The thing I'm most excited about, and also most uncertain about, is the volume question. If you can run thousands of small, cheap investigations, you can explore parts of the research space that nobody would bother with because the expected payoff per experiment is too low for a PhD student to spend a month on. That changes what "worth investigating" means. But it also means the scientific community has to figure out how to deal with a flood of machine-generated work, and I don't think our norms around reviewing and publishing are ready for that yet. So part of what I hope these systems do is force that conversation to happen sooner rather than later.

r001.rationale: The response says human involvement persists and describes human roles in research, but it does not state that humans are required to achieve major scientific breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: It says AI handles more execution and exploration while human taste, judgment, and verification become more important, characterizing the system as increasing the value of those human strengths.

r003.rationale: The response calls for a broader conversation about machine-generated work and mentions building evaluation and guardrails, but does not advocate engaging with these systems early to influence their development.

astra-6.text:
I think the shift is from doing every step of a research project yourself to designing the conditions under which useful research can happen. You still need to ask: What’s an interesting question? What would count as convincing evidence? And where might our evaluation be misleading us?

With v1, the research process was more constrained by a human-provided starting point and structure. V2 moves toward giving the system more freedom to explore and organize its experiments. As that autonomy increases, the human role moves toward setting the research agenda, providing feedback, and critically assessing the results.

But I wouldn’t equate producing a paper with making a scientific discovery. You can automate experiments and writing and still end up with something that isn’t particularly insightful. The exciting possibility is that these systems make it much cheaper to test ideas, including ideas a human wouldn’t have had time to pursue. Then the challenge becomes deciding which results deserve our attention and which claims actually hold up.

r001.rationale: The response describes human roles in setting agendas and evaluating results, but does not state that major scientific breakthroughs still require human involvement.

r002.rationale: It says AI can make testing ideas cheaper, but does not clearly characterize the systems as amplifying humans’ distinctive strengths.

r003.rationale: The response does not advocate engaging with AI research systems early to influence their development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the shift is from doing every individual step yourself to designing the process by which research happens. With AI Scientist v1, there was still quite a lot of human structure around the system: you provided a research direction and a code template, and it could explore ideas, run experiments, and write up the results within that setup. So the human was still defining much of the experimental playground.

With v2, we tried to give the system more freedom in how it explores that space. That moves the human role further toward asking good questions, choosing what is worth investigating, and deciding what counts as convincing evidence.

But I wouldn’t equate generating a paper with making a scientific discovery. You still need to check whether the experiments support the claims, whether the result is robust, and whether it actually teaches us something. My hope is that these systems make it cheap to explore ideas that a researcher wouldn’t otherwise have time to pursue. Then humans can spend more of their attention on interpreting the results and deciding where to go next.

r001.rationale: The response says humans should assess evidence and interpret results, but does not clearly state that major scientific breakthroughs with AI Scientist still require human involvement.

r002.rationale: It describes AI systems making exploration cheaper while humans focus on question selection, judging evidence, and interpreting results, conveying that the systems extend human contributions.

r003.rationale: The response does not advocate engaging with AI research systems early to influence their development.
